newsitem.title: USA: Republicans vow to press Clinton probes.
newsitem.headline: Republicans vow to press Clinton probes.

text.p: Republicans vowed on Wednesday that President Bill Clinton's election victory would not keep them from pressing ahead with investigations of his administration, but the White House said voters were sick of the inquisition.

Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott of Mississippi said there would soon be a new set of investigative hearings on Capitol Hill looking into questions about how Clinton's Democratic Party had been raising funds.

Lott said Republicans were particularly interested in John Huang, a former Commerce Department official said to have raised hundreds of thousands of dollars from Asian business interests and Asian Americans for the Democratic Party.
Huang's activities and those of other officials have raised questions about whether Clinton or his strategists may have peddled White House access and policymaking input to foreign interests.

"Look, we have a normal process of doing things, there's a responsibility perhaps in the Commerce Committee to have some hearings on the Huang matter, what he was doing at the Commerce Department and in terms of fundraising," Lott told NBC's "Today" show.

Since Republicans won majorities in Congress two years ago, Capitol Hill has held a series of probes into the activities of Clinton, his wife and several of his aides and associates, ranging from their past business activities to the White House's handling of FBI files. There are also three independent counsels investigating the White House and present and former Cabinet members.
White House officials poured scorn on the very idea that there would be still more investigations and said Clinton's solid win in Tuesday's presidential election meant voters did not want them.

Chief of Staff Leon Panetta said Congress had found nothing in violation of the law. "If there was any message that came last night it is that the American people rejected, really rejected ... those kind of allegations that went nowhere," Panetta told NBC.

"I would hope that rather than engaging in, again, this kind of personal attack, that the Republican leadership will work with the president to deal with the issues that the American people care about," Panetta said in a separate interview with CNN.

Lott told CNN he thought there should be an independent counsel named to look into the campaign finance issue, in which the Democrats have given back some donations after media reports raised questions about their source.

"It appears there were clearly some illegal foreign contributions. I assume that there will be an independent counsel. The way the law is written I would think that would be almost automatic," Lott said.
Congress has no official role in naming an independent counsel but lawmakers can request one and some Republicans have already done that in the campaign finance saga.
Attorney General Janet Reno said last Thursday she was reviewing the requests. She could ask a special U.S. appeals court to name an independent counsel.
National Republican Chairman Haley Barbour said the "scandals" attached to the Clinton administration were important and Congress had to deal with them seriously.

But Chris Dodd, the Democratic Party's general chairman, said people were tired of the constant headlines about investigations. "I hope these investigations, subpoenas, this stuff will end. I'm telling you, people are sick of it in this country. They want to see people work together," he told CNN.
